title: Agency Begins with Choice
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Schafer argues that many systems and many leaders are oriented toward defending against what they fear rather than creating what they want, and that this keeps people reactive and disconnected from their own agency. She frames agency as the small act of pausing long enough to choose rather than react, one of three key skills in her Leadership Connection Model. Using Einstein and Twain as touchstones, she suggests that fear-driven attention exhausts resources spent on futures that never arrive. She ends with a one-week experiment of noticing where attention goes and asking what one actually wants to create, plus reflection questions.
points: Systems depend on habituated reactions of fear, scarcity and urgency, which leaves leaders reactive rather than creative.
Agency begins not with power or position but with the pause that lets a person choose rather than react.
Fixation on defending against the unwanted leaves little attention for imagining and building what is wanted.
A practical experiment: notice where attention is pulled toward fear for a week, then ask what you want to create instead.
quotes: They depend on our habituated reactions: fear, scarcity, urgency, and the belief that safety comes from control. When we are oriented toward what we don’t want, we become reactive rather than creative.

Agency does not begin with power, position, or authority. It begins with the moment we pause long enough to choose, rather than react, which is why it is one of the three key Leadership Skills in the Leadership Connection Model. When we slow down, discernment returns.

If we are serious about creating the better new, we cannot do so while remaining fixated on defending against the unwanted. When our attention is consumed by what we fear, there is little room left to imagine what we desire, let alone to take the steady steps required to bring it into being.
We fear outcomes that never arrive, yet in the process, we exhaust ourselves and our resources, preparing for them. This loop keeps us stuck: busy, anxious, and disconnected from our own agency.

We can feel the difference between acting from fear and acting from intention. Over time, these small choices accumulate, reshaping how we lead, how we relate, and how we design the systems we participate in.

Notice how often your attention is pulled toward what you fear or wish to avoid. Then, ask yourself what you actually want to create instead. See what changes, in your energy, your clarity, and your sense of agency.
